blocks.h: THE GLOW
Roya Publication No. 50
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Shirin Nouri [shee-REEN noo-REE] brings people into the world for a living. Mehrdad Āstāneh [mehr-DAAD aas-TAA-neh] builds entrances — the eleven seconds in which a person stops being outside a building and starts being inside one. They have a lake, a hut and a boat that leaks, and they have never once fixed it.
Then something arrives that nobody votes for.

It began as a study of women who had spent forty years learning to hold a pleasure instead of spending it. Copied, cultured and delivered in nineteen minutes through a fine tube, it becomes a settlement in the flesh: a continuous, costless ecstasy needing no partner, no occasion and no permission. It does not end.
Offered first to the women for whom nothing has worked, it works. Then it is offered to everyone, then subsidised, then expected, then administered in sleep.
Shirin takes it at forty-seven, with Mehrdad in the room, and he watches the woman he has loved for nineteen years become completely, permanently and genuinely well.
He is left holding a shared past alone, and learns what everybody learns too late: that missing someone is not the price of having had them. It is the last place they still are.
Nobody is persecuted. Nobody is lied to. The instruments are not wrong.
And the old manuals that mapped all of this, eight hundred years before anyone could open a body and look, wrote the method down and left out the last instruction on purpose.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began with an indecent question and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

The ordinary orgasm lasts a few seconds. A small number of people, inside the clinical literature and outside it, report states that run for minutes, for an hour, in rare cases for most of a night. That is an enormous gap inside a single species, and the first thing I wanted to know was how far it goes.
Then the better question arrived underneath it, which is whether the body is built to survive it at all.

Every other appetite comes with a stop. Hunger stops. Thirst stops. Even pain, given long enough, dulls itself and lets you sleep. This one stops too, hard and early, and I could not work out what the stopping was for. It is possible that the brevity is not a limitation. It is possible that the brevity is the design.
Two real traditions sit under this book and I have tried not to muddle them, because almost everybody does.

The Kamasutra [KAA-muh-SOO-truh] is the older of the two and it is not the book it is famous for being. Vatsyayana [vaat-syaa-YUH-nuh] wrote it in Sanskrit, somewhere in northern India, in the early centuries of the common era. It runs to seven books and thirty-six chapters, and the part everybody knows is one book of the seven. The rest is about how to find somebody, how to live with them, how to furnish the room, how to be forgiven. Its whole subject is two people. It never argues for the two; it assumes them, the way you assume a floor.

The chakra [CHUK-ruh] material is a different tradition, centuries later — the tantric and hatha yoga texts, written by people whose interest was not two but one. They wanted to know whether a body could complete its own circuit. They worked on that for a very long time with no instrument except themselves, and I have come to think they solved it, and the solution is the thing this book is frightened of.

What is real: Vatsyayana, the structure and content of his book, the couch with the lute on a peg. The seven stations and their Sanskrit names and literal meanings. The locks, the sealed vessel, the reversal, the claim that the practice stops the burning. The tradition’s insistence that one final instruction was never written down, and the reason they gave.
What is invented is everybody in it, and the thing that is done to them.

I did not want to write about a villain and there isn’t one. Nobody in this book does anything cruel. A good thing is made available to people who need it, and then to people who would merely prefer it, and then it is the water supply — and at no point in that sequence is there a sentence anybody could reasonably refuse.

The part I keep coming back to is the smallest. The old writers were not against pleasure; they were the only people in history who took it seriously enough to spend eight centuries on it. And having built the thing, they looked at what they had built and decided that the dangerous half was not the holding.
It was the not-letting-go. And they would not write that down, because it was the one part that had to be handed over by a person, in a room, to another person who was ready.
I have spent a long time thinking about what a tradition has to know before it does that.

THE BOOK OF DESIRE
Somewhere in northern India, about seventeen hundred years ago, a man sat down to write a book about how to live.

His name was Vatsyayana [vaat-syaa-YUH-nuh]. We know almost nothing else about him. He says at the end of his book that he wrote it in chastity and contemplation, which may be a joke, and may not be, and there is no longer anybody to ask.

He believed that a human life had three things to get right. The first was dharma [DHUR-muh] — doing what you ought to do. The second was artha [UR-thuh] — getting and keeping what you need. And the third was kama [KAA-muh], which has no good English word, and which is the reason you are holding this book.

Kama is pleasure. Not happiness, which is a weather of the mind. Pleasure: the thing that happens in the body when the body is pleased. A peach. Cold water. Music heard rather than listened to. A hand on the back of your neck.

He thought it needed studying, the way medicine needed studying, or architecture, or war. He thought it was difficult and that people were bad at it. And so he wrote his book, and called it the Kamasutra [KAA-muh-SOO-truh] — which means, exactly and unglamorously, the thread of pleasure, a sutra being a thread, the line a teaching is strung along so that it can be carried without being dropped.
It is not the book you think it is.

Seven books, thirty-six chapters, and only one of those books is about what to do with your body. The rest is about how to find somebody. How to make a home. How to behave when you are married, and how to behave when you should not be. How to furnish a room. There is a passage on the correct way to keep a garden, and one on the proper arrangement of a couch — a couch with soft cushions and a canopy, two pillows, a low table, and near it a lute hanging on a peg, because the kind of life Vatsyayana was describing is the kind in which somebody might want a lute at short notice.
He is writing about a whole life with pleasure in it. The famous chapter is twelve pages in a book about everything.
And the thing I want you to carry out of this opening is what he assumed so completely that he never argued for it, the way a man does not argue that water is wet.
He assumed there would be two of you.

Every page of it is two people. The whole architecture of the thing — the approaching, the courting, the quarrelling, the forgiving, the long practical business of sharing a roof with somebody who wants different things at different hours — is a technology for getting one human being into the same room as another and keeping them there. The pleasure is not the achievement. The pleasure is the proof that the difficult thing worked.
He had no idea this would ever need saying.
Now the second tradition, because this is a book about what happened when the two got confused.

Centuries after Vatsyayana — a long way after, five hundred years, a thousand, the dates are argued about and the arguing does not matter here — other people in the same part of the world began writing a different kind of manual.
They were not interested in two of you. They were interested in one.
Their question was not how to give pleasure or receive it. It was stranger, and it is the question this whole history turns on:
What is pleasure for, and what would happen if you did not let it finish?

They had noticed what everybody notices and almost nobody examines, which is that the thing is brief. It builds, it arrives, it is over, and the body afterwards is quiet and a little stupid and glad. Seconds. For something the species organises its entire life around, a handful of seconds.
They wanted to know whether that was a limit or a decision.
So they went looking inside the body for the machinery, with no instruments at all except the body, and they found — or decided, or inherited, and I will not pretend to know which — a map.
The map said: a person is not one thing. A person is a column, and the column has stations.

They called the stations wheels. The word is chakra [CHUK-ruh], and it is not a mystical word at all; it is the ordinary word for a cartwheel, the thing on the ox-cart outside. Seven of them, stacked from the floor of you to the top of your head, each turning on its own, the cart only moving when they turn together.
There is going to be an interlude for each one.

I want to say plainly what they are and what they are not, because the subject attracts a kind of writing that helps nobody. Nobody has ever found a chakra with a knife. They are not organs. What they are is a very old, very careful attempt to describe where things are felt — and on that, which is the only claim they ever actually made, they are extraordinarily accurate. Fear is felt in the belly. Grief is felt in the chest. Shame goes up the throat and stops there. Every language on earth knows this and puts it in its idioms, and these people simply sat down and wrote the list.
So read the interludes as what they are. A field guide to the inside of a person, compiled before anybody could see inside a person, by people who had nothing to work with except being one.
Seven stations. We will climb them one at a time, from the floor to the crown.
I should tell you now that something else climbs them too.
One last thing before we begin, and it is the only promise I will make.

The second tradition solved their problem. That is not a figure of speech and it is not a claim about the supernatural. They found out how to make it last — minutes, then an hour, then in the oldest accounts from dusk until light — and they wrote the method down in careful, patient, unmystical detail, across eight centuries and three scripts, step by step.
And then, at the very end of the sequence, every version of it stops.

There is one final instruction. It is attested everywhere and written nowhere. The commentaries agree that it is short, that it is essential, and that without it the practice is not a practice but an injury. It was never committed to writing in any century. It passed from a living teacher to a living student, in a room, by mouth, and only when the teacher judged the student ready.
They had a reason. They stated it, and it is the one sentence the whole tradition was built to protect, and I have had a very long time to think about it:
The technique must never travel without a person attached.
Hold on to that. You will be given it back.
I. THE LAKE
1. BAIL OR ROW
The boat leaked from the first summer and they never fixed it.

That is where I want to start, because everything else in this history is a consequence, and because of all the facts I hold about Shirin Nouri [shee-REEN noo-REE] and Mehrdad Āstāneh [mehr-DAAD aas-TAA-neh] — and I hold a great many, more than either of them ever knew existed — this is the one I would keep if I were only allowed one.

It was somebody’s uncle’s hut, two hours out of the city, on a lake that had no particular reputation. Pines came down to the water on three sides and stopped a few metres short, so there was a lip of pale stones all the way round, and the stones held the day’s heat until well after dark. The water was cold at the top and colder underneath, and the cold underneath arrived at your ankles without warning, like a hand. At six in the evening the whole surface went the colour of beaten tin and the far shore turned into one unbroken black shape with no trees in it, just a shape, and the light that was left came up at you off the water instead of down from the sky, so that for about forty minutes every clear evening the two of them were lit from below like people on a stage.

The boat was wooden and bad. Somebody had painted it green a long time ago and the green had gone the way green goes. It took on water through a seam near the bow at a rate that Mehrdad, who was an architect and could not help it, measured once with a cup and a watch and announced as a litre every eleven minutes.
Fixing it would have taken an afternoon. There was always something better to do with an afternoon.
So the boat worked like this: one of you rowed and one of you bailed, and you swapped, and if you did not swap at roughly the right time there was a conversation about it.

They had that conversation once, properly, out in the middle, in the second summer. It started as a joke and stopped being one somewhere around the third exchange, and it went on for eleven or twelve minutes and covered, in the way these things do, considerably more ground than a boat. Whose turn it was. Whether keeping track of turns was itself a kind of accounting that a person should be ashamed of. Whether the one who had raised the question had raised it because of the turns or because of a thing that had happened on Tuesday. Whether Tuesday was now on the table.
Tuesday was on the table.

They got back to the hut at dusk with their feet wet, not speaking. He went in and she stayed on the stones. Then she came in, and there was a further ten minutes of the particular silence of two people in one room who have each independently decided to be the better person and are each waiting to be allowed to, and then she said bail or row in a voice that was doing an impression of his voice, and it was not a good impression, and that was the end of it.

For the rest of their lives together the phrase meant about a dozen things. It meant you are keeping score. It meant I am keeping score and I know it. It meant we are having the big argument again in its small costume. It meant, most often, I love you and I am not going to say the long version.

I have the photograph from that summer. It is the only image of either of them that exists anywhere, and it exists because he put it behind glass, and glass is the reason anything from that century survives at all.

She is in the boat. She is bailing, with a plastic cup, badly, because she is laughing at him. There is an inch of lake in the bottom of the boat and the last of the light is in it, so the water inside the boat is brighter than the water outside, and her whole face is lit from underneath by a litre of the leak.
They had three years by then and they were not careful with them, which is the privilege of not knowing how many you are getting.
Shirin was thirty-one and brought people into the world for a living.

She had been a midwife for nine years. It is worth being accurate about what that job is, because the century that followed got very confused about it: she spent her working life in rooms where one body was in the process of becoming two, and the whole of her skill was knowing when to put her hands on and, far more difficult, when to take them off. She had delivered somewhere over four hundred children. She could tell you the sound a room makes in the ninety seconds before a woman stops being frightened and starts working, which is a real sound and is not silence.

She was good at it in a way that had nothing to do with tenderness. She was tender, but that was not the skill. The skill was that she did not look away. Not at the ugly part, not at the frightening part, not at the part where a person you liked said something unforgivable at four in the morning and would not remember it. She stayed in the room with the whole of it and she did not flinch and she did not make it nice, and women asked for her by name for years afterwards, and almost none of them could have told you why.
Mehrdad was thirty-four and built entrances.

That was not the whole job and it was the only part he was good at. Other architects worried about the roof, the load, the money. Mehrdad worried about the eleven seconds in which a person stops being outside a building and starts being inside one — the width of the step, the weight of the door, whether the light came at you as you came through or fell behind you. He had a theory, which he would produce after two drinks and defend after three, that every building in the world is a machine for making somebody welcome or unwelcome, and that most architects are building the second one by accident.

One critic had noticed. Four lines in a trade quarterly that nobody read: Āstāneh builds rooms that expect you. He pretended to be embarrassed about that sentence for the rest of his life. He had it laminated inside the week.

So: she brought people through one threshold and he built the rest of them. Neither of them ever said this out loud to the other, because it is the kind of thing that sounds unbearable said out loud, and because they had better things to talk about, and because they assumed there would be time.
2. THE ORANGE LIGHT
Here is the inside of it, and I am going to take my time and be exact, because this is the thing the rest of the history is measured against and I will not be able to show it to you again.

They were in the hut. It was the hot week of that third summer, the week the pines went sharp and resinous in the afternoons and the stones outside held so much heat that you could still feel it coming off them at midnight through the open door. There was one room and a bed in it and a square window with no curtain, and the window faced west, so from about seven the whole room filled up with a low orange light that came in at the level of the bed and lay across it.
He was describing the light to her. He did that. It was a professional deformation and she had learned to let it run.

And then at some point he stopped describing it, and his hand had been on her hip for a while without either of them making anything of it, and the conversation went somewhere else without anybody deciding.
Start with the warmth, because that is where it starts, and because every account anybody ever wrote of this starts there and then immediately goes vague, and I am not going to go vague.

It is not the warmth of a hot room. A hot room is on the outside of you, arrives everywhere at once, and asks nothing. This begins in one place — low, central, deeper than you expect, four or five centimetres in behind the pubic bone rather than anywhere on the surface — and it has weight. That is the property every description leaves out and it is the one that matters. It is heavy. It has the thickness of warm oil. It does not float; it settles, the way silt settles, and you become aware of the floor of yourself because something is lying on it.
What is physically happening, in the plainest terms, is that she is being flooded.

Arteries that spend the ordinary day half closed are opening along their whole length. Blood is arriving in tissue that is built — this is its actual engineering, it has no other purpose — to receive a great deal of blood very fast and hold it. The tissue swells. It goes from soft to full, and then past full, to a kind of tight ripeness that is the same change a fruit makes in the last day before you pick it. The temperature of her at the core rises by a measurable amount. The whole region becomes heavier, denser, more present — a part of her body that for most of a day registers as approximately nothing begins to register as the heaviest and most occupied thing she owns.

And it gets wet. I am going to say that without decoration because the squeamishness around the word has done real damage to people’s understanding of their own bodies. The flooding pushes clear fluid through the vessel walls and it beads on the inside surfaces the way condensation beads on cold glass, and it keeps coming, and within a minute there is enough of it that the surfaces no longer catch on one another at all and everything slides. That slipperiness is not a side effect and it is not embarrassing. It is the machine reporting that it is ready, in the only language it has, which is liquid.
She felt all of that arrive in the first ninety seconds and could not have told you one word of it.
What she could have told you is that it spread.

Not like heat. Heat moves fast and evenly and thins as it goes. This moved slowly and thickly and did not thin. It went outward along routes already in her, routes she had never once in thirty-one years been aware of, and it filled them the way water fills a dry system — a little at a time, with pressure behind it, so that each new stretch came online fractionally after the one before and she could feel the leading edge of it moving.
Down the inside of the thighs, which is the obvious one.
Up into the low back, which is not, and which is a surprise every time, a broad warm band laid across the kidneys like a hand that has been resting on a radiator.
Out into the soles of the feet, which makes no anatomical sense to anybody who has not had it and perfect sense to anybody who has.

And up. Into the belly, under the ribs, so that her breathing changed without her deciding — shallower, higher in the chest, faster, and then catching, the breath going in in a short hard pull and coming out again as something that was almost a word and was not one.
Now the part that is difficult to explain and that I most want you to have, because everything in this history turns on it.
Her edges stopped being maintained.

In ordinary life you know exactly where you stop. There is a line all the way round you and it is kept up, continuously, at some cost, by a part of the brain that does nothing else: you in here, world out there, border staffed. It is such steady work that you have never noticed it being done, the way you have never noticed your own blink.
The border goes off duty.

Not all at once, and not evenly — it softens in patches, and the patches join up. The place where his hand was stopped being his hand on her hip and became a region of heat and pressure that was not clearly owned by either of them. The sheet under her shoulder stopped being a sheet and became a texture that was happening somewhere, to someone. And because the border is the thing that keeps the world out, the world came in: the orange light stopped being something she was looking at and became something occurring on her, as temperature, on the eyelids and the collarbone; the smell of hot pine came through the open door and did not arrive in her nose, it arrived behind her breastbone; a bird outside landed already inside her head, having skipped the part where you work out what a sound is.

This is what the old writers meant, technically and without any mysticism whatsoever, when they said the stations open from the floor upward. They had no instruments. They had this, and they wrote down what it was like, and what it was like is that a person stops having a boundary and starts having a weather.
Then time stopped working.

Not slowing. Slowing is a dull meeting and it is the opposite of this. Time stopped being a line she was being carried along and became a room she was in, and the room had no clock in it and no door and she was in no hurry to find one. Afterwards she could not say how long. Afterwards she could not reliably say what order things had come in, which alarms people the first few times it happens, and which is not damage: it is simply what the recording equipment does when the body takes priority and the clerk is sent home.
And underneath all of it, driving it, the actual engine:
It builds.
Every pleasure a human being has ever had has a shape and this is the shape. It goes up. Not smoothly — in waves, each one a little higher than the last, and between the waves there is a trough.
The trough is the whole story. Remember the trough.

In the trough, everything that was gathering lets go slightly and slides back down, and what fills the space is wanting. Not wanting in the abstract. A physical, locatable, almost painful emptiness exactly where the fullness had been, with the shape of the fullness still in it, like the dent a body leaves in a bed. And she wanted the next wave more than she has ever wanted anything in her life, and the wanting was itself unbearably good, and this is the paradox at the bottom of the entire species and nobody has ever got past it:
The lack is part of the thing. Remove the lack and you have not improved the pleasure. You have deleted it.

The waves got closer together. That is measurable and it is the reliable sign: the interval shortens, the trough gets shallower, the climb gets steeper. Her hands had stopped being polite some time ago. Her jaw had come open. Somewhere in there she bit him, not hard, on the muscle at the top of the shoulder, and did not know she had done it until he mentioned it two days later in a car.
Her breathing broke into pieces.

And then the building stopped, and there was a half second of absolutely nothing — a flat, bright, airless half second that every person who has had it knows and nobody has ever adequately described, the pause at the lip — and then it arrived.
It is a fist. That is the honest word and the old writers used the same one in three languages.

The muscles of the pelvic floor, the ones she had never once consciously addressed, seized. Not a flex — a seizure, hard, involuntary, and rhythmic, at an interval of about eight tenths of a second, which is a figure I hold for her specifically and which was within the ordinary range for a woman of her age and health. The first contraction is the biggest. It takes the whole hammock of muscle from the pubic bone to the tailbone and closes it like a hand, and everything above it answers: the abdominal wall goes rigid; the deep muscle in the back of the thighs locks; the toes curl so hard the tendons stand up. Eleven of them, for her, that evening. Eight tenths of a second apart, weakening in a smooth decline, so that the last two were more like a shudder than a grip.

And she made a sound she did not choose. That is the thing to understand about this if you have never been there. You do not decide. Sound comes out of a person at the top of this the way water comes out of a pipe when the valve goes, and it is not a performance and it is frequently not attractive and it is one of the very few entirely honest noises a human being makes.
And at the peak of it, for perhaps half a second, Shirin Nouri was not there.

Not unconscious — her eyes were open. Absent. The part of a person that keeps track of being a person, that maintains the running account of I-am-here-and-this-is-happening-to-me, goes offline, and something older and simpler is at the controls. In the imaging of the following century you can watch it happen: whole regions of the front of the brain go quiet, all at once, like a district losing power. The old writers had noticed this without any instrument at all and it is why their accounts are so insistent and so strange. The one who watches is not watching. They thought that was the most important thing about it. They may have been right.
Then she came back.
The afterwards is a physical place and it has its own geography, and nobody writes about it, and it is half of the experience.

The seizing stops but the region does not go quiet. It throbs — a slow, heavy, diminishing pulse, entirely out of time with the heartbeat, which goes on for a minute or two and then becomes an ache and then becomes nothing. The flooding drains slowly, over ten or fifteen minutes, and as it drains the tissue becomes extraordinarily sensitive, so much so that for a short window any touch at all is too much and she pushed his hand away without opening her eyes. There was a tremor in both thighs, high up, which came and went in bursts for about four minutes and which she could not stop and did not try to. Her skin had a film of sweat on it that was already going cold at the shoulders and still hot at the small of the back. She was radiating heat; you could feel it from a hand’s width away, and the room, which had been warm, now felt cool by comparison, and that is not the room changing.

And she was stupid. Pleasantly, completely stupid, for about ninety seconds — unable to assemble a sentence, unwilling to, the whole apparatus of language sitting down on the step outside and waiting to be called back in.

That stupidity costs something. The whole event costs something. She was flattened for the rest of the evening in a way that is close to the feeling after hard physical work, and she slept eleven hours, and the next day she was slightly, obscurely tired at four in the afternoon, and that is the price, and the price was paid, and it was worth it.
The cost is not a flaw. Hold on to that, because it is going to be argued away by people who mean well.
The cost is the receipt.
She said, into the mattress, some minutes later, “The light’s gone.”

It had. The orange had come off the bed while neither of them was available to notice, and the room had turned the grainy blue that comes after, and outside the stones were giving the day’s heat back into a cooling sky, patiently, to an air that had moved on.
Remember the stones. They are the other half of this.
He said he would describe tomorrow’s for her.
She told him to shut up and get the other blanket.
It is necessary to say what this was, because the language for it was lost inside a single lifetime and I want it in the record before I use the word again.

It was not performance. Neither of them was being watched or graded. It was not a transaction; nobody was paying anybody in anything. It was not even, most of the time, especially good — they had ordinary nights, and tired nights, and nights that started and did not finish, and a stretch in the second winter lasting six or seven weeks when something unspoken was wrong between them and the whole apparatus simply went quiet, and then came back, and neither of them ever worked out why it had gone or why it returned.
What it was, was between them.

That is the whole of it. It could not be done alone, it could not be stockpiled, it could not be bought, and it did not survive the removal of either party. It was a thing that existed in the space between two bodies and nowhere else, and it had to be made again every time, out of whatever the two of them had that day, and some days they did not have enough.

Four hundred years later I can tell you the exact chemical cascade, the vessel diameters, the firing rates, the recovery intervals, for that evening, for those two people. I hold the complete description.

I do not hold the thing. There was never a way to hold the thing. That is not a limitation of my archive; it was not holdable by anybody, which is why it had to be made fresh, which is why they went to the lake.
The last summer at the hut was the sixth one.

Nothing happened in it that anybody recorded, and that is the point of including it. They swam. He burned a pan. She slept in the afternoon with one arm over her eyes and he sat in the doorway with a pencil and drew the doorway, badly, from the inside, which is the only drawing of his that survives in private hands and which is, as a piece of architecture, worthless.

On the last evening they took the boat out and got halfway across before the leak made itself felt, and there was no cup in the boat, because somebody had taken the cup up to the hut and not brought it back.

So they sat in the middle of a lake in a boat that was filling, in the forty minutes of light that came up off the water, and did the arithmetic, and worked out that a litre every eleven minutes against the freeboard they had gave them something over an hour, which was more than enough, and that there was therefore no reason at all to hurry.
Nobody rowed. Nobody bailed.
They sat there until the light went, lit from below, in a boat slowly filling with water, and they talked about nothing that anybody wrote down, and it was the best evening of both of their lives.
She was thirty-four that autumn. The first announcements came the following spring.
INTERLUDE · THE FIRST WHEEL — THE ROOT
Muladhara [moo-laa-DHAA-ruh]. It means root-place, and it sits at the very floor of you, at the base of the spine, between the legs, in the hammock of muscle that holds everything in.

You have met it. Everybody has met it. It is the part of you that handles the four things no creature survives without: eating, emptying, running away, and making more. It wants without asking permission and it does not take instruction. It has been doing its job since before there were faces.
Why did the old writers start here, rather than somewhere more flattering?

Because it is the floor. You cannot build upward from a floor you have not found. And because in the specific problem they were working on — holding a pleasure instead of spending it — this is the drain. This is where it falls out. A sensation gathers in a person the way water gathers in a boat, and it runs to the lowest point, and at the lowest point there is an opening, and out it goes.
They had a word for the thing that falls. Bindu [BIN-doo] — the drop. The whole of the second tradition is one instruction about that drop, and the instruction is: do not let it.
So the first lesson is the first lesson in plumbing, and it is not romantic: find the floor, and learn to close it.

They called the closing the mūla bandha [MOO-luh BUN-duh] — the root lock, the first of three, bandha meaning simply a binding. It is nothing more mystical than the movement you already make to stop yourself, performed on purpose and held for a very long time.

Alongside the locks they set the hands. A mudrā [MOO-draa] is a seal: a fixed arrangement of the fingers held throughout the practice, dozens of them catalogued, each said to close a different circuit. The plainest reading of them is one the manuals never give and I will. A body with its hands occupied is a body that has agreed not to leave.

The ring of muscle is real, you own it, and you have almost certainly never thought about it on purpose. It is the one you use to stop yourself at an inconvenient moment. Tighten it now, lightly, and let it go. There. That is the first gate of the oldest technology anybody ever built out of a human being, and you just operated it while reading.

What does control of this wheel give you? The old manuals are blunt. It gives you a vessel that does not leak. Nothing else they teach works without it, in the same way that nothing you do to a bucket matters until you have dealt with the hole.
And they say one more thing about the root, and they say it in every version, and it took me a long time to understand that it is a warning rather than an instruction.

Something sleeps down there. They call it the coiled one — kundalini [koon-duh-LEE-nee] — and they are insistent that this is not a figure of speech for a feeling. They describe an animal. It has weight. It lies in three and a half turns at the base of the spine with its head down over the opening, like a stopper, and it sleeps your entire life.
Close the floor and the water has nowhere to go.
It rises.
And the thing at the bottom, which has been asleep for your whole life with its head over the drain, turns over.
3. NOTHING IN YOUR FACE
The announcement was not an announcement. That is the first thing to understand about how this arrived, and almost nobody at the time understood it, and the few who did were in no position to say so.

There was no launch, no press conference, no man at a podium. There was a slow accumulation of small items over about two years: a trial result in a journal nobody reads; a regulatory approval reported in four lines on a financial page; a feature in a weekend supplement with a photograph of a woman in a kitchen looking well. The feature used the phrase for women for whom nothing has worked, and it was not lying, and that was the whole of its power.
What had been built was this, and I will give it to you in the plainest terms available, because the century it came out of spent eighty years not saying it plainly.

Somewhere there had been a study of women who had spent decades on the second tradition’s practice — the holding — and in the oldest of them, the ones with thirty and forty years behind them, somebody had found that the body had been doing something. Small pale structures had formed in the tissue, arranged along the nerves, regular, organised, not a disease. The body, asked to host an enormous visitor for four decades, had quietly begun building it a room.

The structures were copied. A cell line was made from them — the line, which is what a cell culture is called and also what a family is called, and nobody involved enjoyed the coincidence. It was stripped of everything that pointed toward a child, and this one thing the century did carefully, and verified it twice. What was left was the other inheritance: the slow pulse, the warmth, the body’s own supply of its own comforts, running continuously, at low volume, forever.

It was delivered in nineteen minutes through a fine tube, and it settled into one kind of tissue and no other, and it spread along the paths already there, slowly, respectfully, the way ivy follows a wall it has decided to love.
And it copied itself, because the originals had copied themselves, and faithfulness to the source was the entire point.

The women who had it called it the Glow within about a year, and the name came from one of them trying to explain it and giving up and saying it was less like a feeling than like a light left on somewhere in the house.
Nobody called it anything else after that.
Mehrdad found out about it in a bar from a colleague, the way everybody found out about everything.
Shirin found out about it at work, which was different, and which is why she thought about it for two years before she said anything at the kitchen table.

She was a midwife. The first carriers she met were patients — women who had the thing and were having a child anyway, in the early years when that still overlapped — and she watched them labour. She would not discuss it with anybody for a long time and when she finally did discuss it, with him, at the table, she did it in order and without decoration, the way she did everything that mattered.
“They don’t do the sound,” she said.
“What sound?”

“There’s a sound.” She was turning a glass. “About an hour in, there’s a sound women make when they stop being frightened and start working. Every room. Every country. It’s not a scream, it’s lower than that, it’s —” and she did it, briefly, at the table, a low open note with no edges on it, and then stopped, embarrassed, because it is not a thing you do in a kitchen.
“And they don’t?”
“They don’t need to.” She put the glass down. “They’re not frightened. They’re not anything. The whole labour goes past them like weather. I had one in March who read for most of it.”
“That sounds —” he started, and then didn’t finish, because he could hear where the sentence was going and it was going somewhere good, and he could tell from her face that good was not the finding.

“It sounds wonderful,” Shirin said. “I know. Say it, it’s fine, it is wonderful. I have watched four hundred women do the worst day of their lives and I would take the pain off every one of them if I could, and I’m telling you that the three of them in March went through it like a tunnel on a train.”
She looked at the window.

“And at the end they held the baby, and they were glad. Genuinely. Not pretending. And I stood there with my hands still wet and I thought: there’s nothing in your face. And then I thought — and this is the bit I’ve not said to anybody, so don’t be clever about it — I thought, who is going to tell her what she did? Because nobody else was in the room. And she isn’t going to know. And in a year she’ll have been told she had a nice time.”
4. YOU STAYED

Here is their life in those years, because they had one, and because a history that only records the turning points is a lie about how a turning point feels from inside, which is: like nothing, on a Tuesday.

They had a flat on the fourth floor with a bad kitchen. They had a standing argument about whether the kitchen was bad, which Mehrdad maintained was the best-proportioned room either of them had ever lived in and which Shirin maintained had been designed by somebody who had never once cooked. Neither position was abandoned in nineteen years.

They had Tuesday wine with the woman from the floor below, a court stenographer, tall and loud and funny, whose whole personality was an open circuit — she wanted at volume, all the time, everything, and had built a self out of the wanting the way coral builds a reef.
They had the lake, less often as the years went, because of work, which is how it goes.

And they had, in the fourteenth year, a stretch of about eight months in which Shirin did not sleep properly, because of a night in February with a woman she could not save, and the whole machinery of the two of them went into a kind of shutdown that neither had experienced before. He did not fix it. There was nothing to fix. He cooked, badly. He sat in the room with her and did not say anything useful, for eight months, and some nights she was angry at him for being there and said so, and he stayed anyway because the alternative was leaving and he had worked out, in the first fortnight, that there was no third option and that waiting was not nothing.

I have to give you February, because the summary above is a lie of the kind that histories tell, and because everything the next four hundred years did to the human body is in the space between the sentence a woman she could not save and the four hours it actually took.
Her name was Marta and she was thirty-six and she had wanted the child for eleven years.

The delivery was unremarkable and the baby was fine and the room was, for about ninety seconds, the best room in the building. Then the bleeding started, and it was the kind that does not announce itself — no crisis, no alarm, a quantity of blood that is normal, and then a quantity that is at the upper end of normal, and then a figure that is not a figure anybody says out loud, arriving in increments, each of which could be the last one.

Shirin did everything. I have the record and I have checked it against the standard of the period and against the standard of every period since, and she did everything, in the right order, inside the right intervals, and she was the one who called it early, nine minutes before the attending agreed with her.

It made no difference. There are bodies that do this. The vessels do not close. The muscle that is supposed to clamp down on the open ground where the placenta was does not clamp down, and the drugs that make it clamp down do not make it clamp down, and a woman bleeds out through a wound the size of a dinner plate that is on the inside of her and cannot be pressed.

Four hours. Marta was conscious for most of them, and lucid for most of that, and she knew, somewhere in the third hour, in the way they always know. And what she did with the knowing was ask about the feeding.

That is the part Shirin could not get out of her afterwards. Not the blood. She had seen oceans of blood; blood was Tuesday. It was that a woman at the end of her own life, with four hours left and no way to be wrong about it, spent eleven of her minutes asking a midwife to make sure the child was put to somebody, because a baby that has not fed in the first hours does not do as well, and she had read that, and she was not going to be there to do it.

Shirin held her hand and told her it was arranged. It was not yet arranged. She arranged it at six in the morning, from the corridor, with her shoes in a bag because her shoes were not shoes any more.
The child lived. The child was fine.

And every year after that, on the date, Shirin Nouri said Marta’s name out loud once, usually in a kitchen, usually to nobody, in the flat tone of a woman reading a meter. Mehrdad knew what the date was and never once mentioned it. I hold every one of them. There are twenty-one.
I know the year they stop. I am going to tell you, and it is not the year you would guess, and it is not the molt.
Then the eight months, and they do not have a story, which is what nobody writes down about grief.
There is no arc to it. It does not deepen or resolve. It is the same Tuesday, administered one hundred and ninety times.
Here is one of them, and it stands for the rest because they were interchangeable, which was the worst of their properties.

Three in the morning in the fourth month. She is awake because she is always awake at three in the morning now, and the waking is not dramatic — no gasp, no dream, she simply arrives at consciousness fully assembled and already in the middle of it, the way you arrive in a room where a conversation has been going on without you. She is lying on her side looking at a wall she knows every centimetre of. The thing in her chest is not sadness. Sadness is a feeling and has a shape. This has no shape. It is a physical heaviness in the sternum and a tightness along the jaw and a sensation of being slightly too large for her own skin, and it goes on being those things for about four hours, at which point it is light and she gets up and goes to work and delivers other people’s children, competently, all day.

He is awake too. She knows he is awake because the breathing is wrong. He has been awake for three months at three in the morning and has never once said so, having worked out in the first fortnight — the exact phrase is his, from a page I hold, written much later — that a man in the room is furniture or he is a witness, and the difference is whether he can keep his mouth shut.
Some nights she took his hand.
That night she said, without turning round, in a voice with nothing in it, “You can go and sleep in the other room. You’re not helping.”
And he said, “No.”

And that was the whole exchange, and she was furious, and the fury was the first thing with any heat in it she had felt in four months, and she lay in it and did not thank him for a further five months, and then thanked him for the rest of her natural life.
I want to be plain about what was happening in that bed, because the century that came next could not have described it and would not have believed it was a good.

Two people were lying in the dark, awake, in pain, getting nothing. No relief was being provided. No problem was being solved. Nothing was improving. And the whole of what was occurring — the entire content of the event — was that one of them was not alone, and the only mechanism by which she was not alone was that there was another body in the room that could have left and had not.
That is it. That is the whole machine. It has no parts.

It cannot be subsidised, delivered in nineteen minutes, or administered in sleep, and when the century finally built something that could, it built it for the other thing — for the pleasure, which is loud and measurable and sits in two stations at the bottom of a person — and nobody ever thought to ask what else had been running on the same wire.

In the ninth month she came home and sat down on the edge of the bed and told him about February, properly, all of it, for about two hours, and at the end of it she cried in a way she had not managed to since the night itself.
And this is the part I need you to hold, because the century that came afterwards would not have been able to parse it:
That was the best thing that ever happened to them.

Not the lake. Not the hot afternoon with the orange light. The eight bad months and the two hours at the end of them, because the eight months were the proof and the two hours were the receipt, and a thing that costs nothing cannot pay for anything.
She told him so. She said, “You stayed.”
And he said, “Bail or row,” and she laughed with her face completely wet, and that was the summit of two human lives, and nobody photographed it.
5. THE HOT AFTERNOON
The Kamasutra came into the flat in the sixteenth year, and it came in as a joke.

Somebody had given it to her at a work thing — the good edition, the heavy one with the apparatus, which is not a gift anybody gives seriously — and it sat on the shelf for most of a year before a hot Sunday when neither of them could be bothered to go out and she took it down to be funny.
She read him the chapter on the couch.

A couch, soft, and not too high, with a canopy above it, and two pillows, one at the head and one at the foot. Near it a stand for the night’s ointments and garlands, and on the wall a lute, hanging from a peg.
“A lute,” Mehrdad said. “On a peg.”
“On a peg.”
“In case.”
“In case,” Shirin agreed.

And he laughed so hard that he had to put his drink down, and she read on in the voice of a man reading out a tender document, and for about forty minutes the hot afternoon in the fourth-floor flat was the best room in that city.
Then she stopped laughing, somewhere in the fourth book, and read for a while without saying anything.
“What?”
“It’s not a sex book,” she said.
“It’s famously a sex book.”

“It’s famously twelve pages of a sex book.” She turned back and forward. “The rest of it is — Mehrdad, it’s about how to live with somebody. It’s how to behave when you’re married. It’s what to do when she’s angry and you don’t know why. There’s a bit here about how to be forgiven.” She read it out. It was practical and slightly cynical and seventeen hundred years old and it was, in every particular, advice that would have worked on either of them.
“He assumes there’s two of you,” she said at last. “He doesn’t even argue it. He assumes it the way you’d assume there’s a floor.”
She put the book down on her chest and looked at the ceiling, and outside the window the city made the noise it made.
“I’ve started saying no to women,” she said.
He waited.

“Not saying no. I’m not — I don’t have the standing to say no. They come in and they’ve already decided and they want me to tell them it’s fine, because I’m the one who’s seen the inside of things.” She was still looking at the ceiling. “Two this month. And I said what I’m supposed to say, which is that it’s their body and the evidence is good, and both times I came out into the corridor and stood there.”
“And thought what?”

“That I don’t have a sentence.” She turned her head. “That’s the whole problem, that’s the entire problem, right there. They’ve got one. They’ve got nothing has ever worked and this works. And I’ve got — what? A noise women make at four in the morning? A book with a lute in it?”
She put her arm over her eyes, the way she did.
“Somebody’s going to ask me properly one day,” she said, “and I’m going to have nothing, and I’m going to say yes.”
It was the sixteenth year. She was forty-four. The waiting list opened to the general public eleven months later and ran, in that city, to four hundred thousand names inside a season.
INTERLUDE · THE SECOND WHEEL — THE SWEET PLACE

Svadhisthana [svaa-dhish-THAA-nuh]. The name means one’s own dwelling — her own place, the place that belongs to her — and it sits a hand’s width below the navel, low in the belly, behind and above the root.

This is the water wheel. Every old account gives it the moon and the sea and the colour of deep water, and they are not being decorative: this is the station of everything in a person that is fluid. Desire. Appetite. The pull toward another body. The making of children. Tears, which is not a coincidence and which every one of those writers noticed.
If the root is the part that wants without asking, this is the part that wants somebody in particular.

Put your hand flat below your navel. Something lives under there, and you have felt it move. It is what drops when you see a face you were not expecting. It is what turns over at a certain voice. It is the hollow sensation that the English language insists on calling butterflies, which is a child’s word for the most consequential feeling an adult ever has.
Why did they put it in the scriptures?

Because this is where the trouble is. The root is simple; the root wants and is satisfied and sleeps. This one is never satisfied, because what it wants is not a thing, it is a person, and a person cannot be consumed and so cannot be finished with. Every tradition that ever tried to get a human being to behave has had to come through this room and most of them tried to lock it. The second tradition did not lock it. They thought that was stupid, and said so, and the first thing they teach about this wheel is that you cannot climb past a floor you have refused to stand on.
What does control of this wheel give you?

The manuals are specific and it is not what people expect. It does not give you less desire. It gives you desire that you can carry. The untrained version of this wheel spills — it goes toward whoever is in front of it, it empties itself at the first opportunity, it is enormous and brief. Trained, it becomes something you can hold full without having to pour out: the difference between a man who must drink the water now and a man who can carry the bucket up a hill.
And here, exactly here, is where the whole catastrophe of this history is going to happen, so let me set it down while we are standing in the room.

The thing that came later settled in this station first. Not the root, not the heart. Here, in the sweet place, the room that belongs to her, the one wheel in the body whose entire function is the pull toward another person — and it filled that room so completely and so warmly and so permanently that there was no longer any space in it for the pull.
The old writers would have understood what happened immediately. They had a word for a flooded field.
They did not have a word for a field that is glad.
II. THE OFFER
6. THE WAITING LIST
The woman from the floor below went in first, and that is how it came into their house: not as an argument but as a neighbour.

The stenographer. Tall, loud, funny, the open circuit. She had wanted at volume for twenty years — jobs, men, a particular flat on a particular street, a holiday she talked about for a decade and never took — and she had built an entire personality out of the wanting, the way coral builds a reef out of the thing it cannot stop secreting.
She told them at Tuesday wine, in the way you announce a holiday.
“Second of next month,” she said. “I’m forty-four and I’ve been waiting for my life to start since I was nineteen and I have decided to stop waiting.”
Shirin asked the midwife’s question, which was not why.
“What have they told you about taking it out?”
“That it’s straightforward in the first year.” She refilled her glass. “Don’t do the face.”
“I’m not doing a face.”

“You’re doing the face you do at work. I’ve seen it. It’s the face that means I’ve read the notes and you haven’t.” She was laughing. She was genuinely, uncomplicatedly happy, and it is important to say that, because the accounts afterwards made all of this furtive and it was not furtive; it was Tuesday, and there was wine, and a woman in her forties had found something that was going to help.
Ten days after, Shirin met her on the stairs and knew before a word.

It was not a glow in the way the word suggests — nothing shone, nothing was lit. It was a stillness. The stenographer had always occupied a stairwell the way weather occupies a valley, and now she stood in it, pleasantly, completely at rest, with the particular quality of a person who is not waiting for anything at all.
“Well?” Shirin said.
She considered the question with an attention she had never in twenty years given any question.
“I keep starting to tell you about it,” she said, “and then not needing to.”
That was the year the thing stopped being a treatment.
The sequence is worth setting down in order, because every step was defensible and the sum of the steps was not, and because nobody anywhere ever voted for the sum.
First it was for women for whom nothing had worked, and that was true, and it worked.
Then it was for women for whom something had worked but not well, which is a larger group, and which includes, if you ask the question in the right way, nearly everybody.

Then the insurers found that carriers cost less. Not in any sinister way — they simply presented at the clinic less, took fewer of a certain class of medication, and reported, on every instrument anybody had, that they were well. The instruments were not wrong. That is the sentence this whole decade keeps arriving at and it should be printed once in plain type: the instruments were not wrong. The carriers were, by every measure the century possessed, better off.
Then it was subsidised, and the waiting list in that city ran to four hundred thousand names in a season.
And then, within about two years, not having it became a thing you could be asked about.

Not by the state. By a colleague, pleasantly, in a corridor. By a sister. By a woman at a dinner who said oh, you haven’t? and then was perfectly nice about it for the rest of the evening, which was worse.
Mehrdad watched this from a particular angle, because by then his work had started to go, and he was the sort of man who noticed the shape of a thing before he noticed what it meant.

Residential went first. Nobody was commissioning flats; they were converting them. The conversions wanted retrofit engineers rather than architects, and what they were converting them into was a thing the industry had started calling a pod — a sealed residence, climate-held, fed through a line, lit from inside, waste reclaimed.
He went to look at one, early, while they were still showing them.
He stood in the doorway for a long time and the sales agent, who was good, left him alone.
Then he said, “There’s no threshold.”
“Sorry?”

“There’s no —” He moved his hand at the opening, which was a smooth continuous curve from corridor to interior, no step, no frame, no change of material. “You don’t arrive. You’re outside it and then you’re inside it and nothing happens in between.”
“That’s the design,” the agent said, pleased, thinking he had understood. “No barriers.”
Mehrdad went home and sat on the edge of the bath for some time.

He had spent his whole working life on the eleven seconds in which a person stops being outside and starts being inside, and he had believed — he had built a career on believing — that a door is a machine for making somebody welcome. And he had just stood in a doorway designed by people who had correctly understood that if nobody is ever going to arrive, you do not need a door. You need an aperture.
A pod is not a room that expects you, he wrote that night, in the margin of a drawing nobody had commissioned. It is a room that replaces the need to be expected.

He showed Shirin. She read it twice and put the drawing down and did not say anything for a while, and then she said, “Say that to me again in ten years,” which was meant kindly and was the single most frightening sentence of his life, and he did not understand why until much later.
They had it out at the kitchen table in the nineteenth year, in the bad kitchen, over two evenings.

I have no recording of this. There is no file. Two people talked in a room with the window open and nobody wrote it down, and the fact that I cannot give it to you verbatim is the single greatest gap in everything I hold, and I have had a very long time to sit with that.
What I have is what each of them said about it afterwards, separately, years apart, to other people. So this is reconstruction and I will mark it as such. It is close. It is not the thing.

She said: I am going to say the true reason and not the good one. The good one is that I’m forty-seven and my work is a body breaking in half and I am tired in a way sleep doesn’t touch. That’s true and it’s not why.

She said: The why is that I was in a corridor in March and a woman I’d just delivered said thank you, and I had nothing underneath my face. Nothing. I did the voice and the hand on the arm and I was somewhere else entirely, and I have been somewhere else for about two years, Mehrdad, and you haven’t said, and I love you for not saying, and it has to stop.
He said — and this is the part he repeated, decades later, in rooms where it no longer meant anything — Then stop. Take six months. Take a year, we have money, take the lake.
And she said the thing that ended it, which was not cruel, and which was, as far as I can determine, entirely accurate:
You are offering me a rest. I am telling you the floor is gone.
On the second evening he tried the only argument he actually had, and he made it badly, because he was not a man who could make this kind of argument and he knew it while he was doing it.
He said that he did not want to be left on the other side of it.
And she said, “You won’t be.” And then, because she did not lie to him: “I don’t think you will be.”
And then, after a while: “Do you want me to not?”

And Mehrdad Āstāneh, fifty years old, in a kitchen he had always maintained was well proportioned, with the whole of his life on the table in front of him, said the sentence that he would take out and look at for the next thirty years the way you take out a stone you brought with you:
“I want you to want to not.”
She reached over and put her hand flat on the back of his hand and left it there.
“I know,” she said. “That isn’t a thing I can do for you.”
7. NINETEEN MINUTES
It took nineteen minutes and there was no ceremony and no theatre.

She lay on a table in a bright room. A fine tube went where it needed to go — the whole procedure is done from inside, through the wall, with a needle you would struggle to see at arm’s length — and a quantity of something far too small to deserve the word dose was left in the tissue, and then it was over and she was told she could dress.

What had been put into her was about four hundred thousand cells. They would find the paths that were already there, and settle along them, and begin doing the one thing they had been built to do, which was to produce — steadily, modestly, continuously, each cell contributing almost nothing — the chemistry the body makes for itself at the top of pleasure.

One cell’s output is nothing. Four hundred thousand is a climate. And they copy themselves, so by the end of the first week there would be eleven million, and by the end of the first year the number stops being a useful way to think about it.
The sheet said resume normal activity.
So she thanked the nurse, and went down to the street, and got on a tram, because Shirin Nouri followed protocols.
It began between the Kunsthaus and the bridge.

She was standing in the aisle with one hand on the rail when the first of it arrived, and it arrived the way the tide arrives in a place with no beach: all at once, from underneath, with no warning at the edges.

It began low and deep behind the bone — the same place the warmth had always begun, the exact place, which is one of the cruelties of the design — and it had the same weight to it, the same thick settling quality, the pressure of a wide flat hand laid against her from the inside.
Then it spread, and it spread wrong.

Not wrong in any way she could have objected to. Wrong in the way a flood is wrong: it did not follow the paths in order, pausing at each one, arriving as a front you could feel moving. It came up everywhere at once, from below, as a level. One moment the warmth was in one place and the next moment it was in all the places, at the same depth, at the same temperature, as though a tank had filled.

The flooding was the same flooding. Vessels opening along their length; tissue going from soft to full and then past full to that tight ripeness; the core temperature climbing; the slipperiness arriving within the minute and continuing to arrive. Her body did every single thing it had ever done in the orange light of a hut by a lake, correctly, in the right order, with nobody there.
Her grip closed on the rail. A man glanced up and then away.
And then it kept going.
That is the sentence the whole century hangs on and I want it to sit by itself.

She knew what the top of this was. Everybody knows. It builds, it waits, it seizes, it empties. She had been there several thousand times in her life and she knew the shape of the road and roughly where she was on it, and she waited, standing in the aisle of a tram at twenty past three in the afternoon, for the fist.
It came, and came, and it did not close.

The muscles that had always slammed shut in a short hard series of eleven took hold instead of a long rolling tension that would not put itself down. Deep in her, fibres she had no names for began to twitch on their own schedule, two or three a second, asynchronous, each one firing a small warm pulse up the spine and down the inside of the thigh — and because they were not in time with one another there was no rhythm to ride, and because there was no rhythm there was no crest, and because there was no crest there was no end.

Every breath took it higher and then let it down, and each time it came down it settled lower than it had started. Her heart pushed another wave through. Then another. Nothing was being spent, so everything accumulated.
And the troughs did not come.

That was the part she could not make sense of afterwards and never could. All her life the waves had been separated by that small bearable emptiness, the dent in the bed, the wanting — and now the waves arrived on top of one another with nothing between them, no slack, no hollow, no place where she was not full.

She understood, distantly, in the part of her that stayed on duty no matter what was happening to the rest, that she should sit down. There were seats. She did not take one, because sitting down would have meant something, and she had not yet decided what was happening.

So she stood in the aisle of a tram in the middle of the afternoon with her coat on and her bag against her hip, while something that had no business lasting this long went on not finishing, and the city went past the window in the ordinary way, and a woman near the doors did a crossword.
It had no shape.

That is the finding and she filed it with the last of the part of her that filed things. Every pleasure she had ever had was shaped — it went up, it arrived somewhere, it came down, and the shape was how you knew where you were inside it. This had no shape. It was a volume, and it was still filling, and there was no edge anywhere in it to push against and find out how much room was left.
At some point she noticed that her jaw had come unclenched. She had not known it was clenched. It had been clenched, she thought, for about two years.

She rode past her stop. She rode past the next one. She got off at the terminus, at the edge of the city, with no memory of the middle eleven minutes, and stood on the pavement in the cold with her hand still curled in the shape of the rail, radiating heat, and laughed out loud, once, at nothing, like a woman who has just got away with something.
INTERLUDE · THE THIRD WHEEL — THE JEWEL CITY
Manipura [MUH-nee-POO-ruh]. It means the city of jewels, which is a strange and gorgeous name for the pit of your stomach, and they chose it on purpose.
It sits behind the navel and just above it, in the soft triangle under the ribs where, if you press, you can feel your own pulse. This is the fire wheel. Every account gives it the sun.
And it is the first one you have ever consciously used.

The root wants. The sweet place wants somebody. This one does something about it. It is the part of you that decides, pushes, goes, refuses. When you say you had no stomach for something, you are reporting on this wheel with complete accuracy. When fear arrives, it arrives here, as a drop and a cold loosening, and the drop is this wheel being overruled. When you have made up your mind and will not be moved, there is a hard quiet knot here, and you can find it with your hand.

It is also, straightforwardly, where you burn your food. The old writers knew that and did not consider it a separate fact. Digestion, will, courage and heat were one subject to them, and the more I have turned that over the less primitive it looks: a fire that converts what you take in into what you can do is the same fire whichever end of it you stand at.
Why did it go into the scriptures?

Because this is the wheel that drives. The practice they were building needed something to push the gathered sensation upward against its own weight, and this is the only part of a person that pushes. They were quite practical about it. Close the floor, they said, and then draw the belly back and up under the ribs — an actual physical movement, which you can do now, which pulls the whole cavity up and in and makes the vessel smaller — and what is inside the vessel has nowhere to go but up. That is the second lock, the uddiyāna bandha [oo-DEE-yaa-nuh BUN-duh], and the name means the flying up, which is precisely what it is for.

Control of this wheel gives you, in their terms, the capacity to be undiverted. A person with a weak fire is blown about by whatever arrives. A person with a strong one can hold a course through discomfort — can sit in the trough, which is the hardest instruction in the entire system, and not reach for the thing that would end it.
I want to note something here and then leave it alone.

In the old sequence, the fire is above the sweet place, and this matters: the drive sits above the desire and can therefore act on it. The sun is above the water and can raise it as vapour. That is the ladder they built.
The engineered version did not use this wheel at all. It had no need of a drive, because nothing had to be pushed anywhere; the warmth was simply manufactured in place, below, forever, at no cost.
For generations afterwards, in forty million bodies, the fire wheel sat above a sea that never needed raising, with nothing to burn and nothing to lift, like a sun over a flooded country.
What happens to a fire with no work is in the next part of this book.
8. THE SETTLING
It banked down over the following days into the thing it would be for the rest of her life.
Here is what that was, physically, hour by hour, and I am going to be exact because the official literature of that century stood politely on every side of this and touched it nowhere.
There is no peak to chase, because the peak has moved in and unpacked.
The Glow does not knock, does not build, does not arrive and leave. It is not an event in the body; it is the weather of the body, and it is always four o’clock on a warm afternoon.

The baseline is a full, heavy, open sensation from the pubic bone to the top of the thighs — not the sharp localised ache of wanting, but a broad occupied warmth, as though she had been resting a hot water bottle there for an hour and then taken it away and the heat had stayed. It is always there. It is there when she wakes. It is the first thing she is aware of and it does not require her attention and it does not go away when she gives her attention to something else.

On top of the baseline there are the fibres, which never stop. Small involuntary twitches, deep, two or three a second, never in time with each other — and because they are never in time, the effect is not rhythm but a kind of continuous low shimmer, like a field of grass with wind going over it in several directions at once.

The tissue is permanently slightly swollen and permanently slightly wet. Not dramatically. Enough that she is always aware of it, that everything down there always slides a little, that there is a faint sweetish smell on her skin at the end of a day which no soap entirely takes off and which other carriers can detect on each other across a room, a fact never once written into any official document and known to every woman who had it.
And then the ordinary business of being alive becomes, permanently, a mild sexual event.
Walking is a soft internal friction, step after step, for as long as she walks.
Sitting down is a slow private undulation that lasts about four seconds and happens every time she sits down, for the rest of her life.

A full bladder is pressure and pleasure at once and becomes genuinely difficult to distinguish, so that the body’s signal to go to the lavatory arrives as something she does not immediately want to act on.

Cold air on the backs of the legs. The seam of a chair. The vibration of a vehicle, which she stopped being able to ride without a particular effort of attention for about the first two years and then simply stopped noticing, the way you stop noticing a river you live beside.

Sleep does not interrupt it. Sleep turns it down. It goes on underneath, in the dark, breathing low, patient as a second pulse, and she dreams inside it, and wakes into it, and the join between sleeping and waking becomes soft and unimportant in a way that she found, in the first months, almost unbearably luxurious.
And it does not spend itself.

That was the part nobody had a word for. Every pleasure Shirin had known in her life had been a small purchase made against a small fund, and afterwards there was less. This took nothing. It was the first warmth she had ever been inside that did not cost.
He was in the flat for all of it, which is a thing the later accounts leave out.

They did not separate. Not for years. He was there in the first week, when she could not stop smiling at the ceiling; there in the first month, when she slept better than she had in a decade and woke looking twenty-nine; there in the fourth month, when she said, out of nowhere, over a pan, “I haven’t had a bad hour since March,” and he said good, and meant it, and did not sleep that night.
And he watched, because he was a man who watched thresholds for a living, and because something in the room had changed its proportions and he could not yet say what.
What he noticed first was not sexual. It was the pauses.

Shirin had always been a person who, in a conversation, was coming. You could feel her assembling the next thing while you were still talking, leaning fractionally in, the whole apparatus of her running slightly ahead. It had been exhausting at times and he had complained about it and he had loved it with his entire chest.
Now she listened, completely, and at the end of what he said there was a pause.
Not a rude pause. A pause in which nothing was being assembled, because nothing needed to be. She would answer, warmly, accurately, and she would not have been waiting to.

He found that he had begun to talk more, to fill it. He noticed himself doing it one evening and stopped mid-sentence and felt obscurely humiliated, which was unreasonable, and he knew it was unreasonable, and he went and stood in the kitchen.
Then the thing that is difficult to say.

They still went to bed. For some years. She was affectionate, and warm, and present, and generous — markedly more generous than she had been in the bad years, because nothing cost her anything now and there was no reason to be careful with it.

And the first time she came, under his hands, in the ordinary way, three months in, it happened quickly and easily and she made the old sound and afterwards she lay there with an expression he had never seen on her face in nineteen years.
“What?” he said.
She was looking at the ceiling, running the finding the way she ran everything.
“It didn’t do anything,” she said.
She turned her head and saw his face and reached over immediately, which is the detail that tells you she had not yet changed, because the old Shirin would have done exactly that.

“That came out wrong. It was lovely. I mean it did not —” and she searched, with real effort, for a way to put it that would not take anything off him, and found one, and the one she found was worse than the thing she was avoiding. “It’s like striking a match in a lit room.”
They were both quiet for a bit.
“Is the room lit all the time?”
“Yes,” Shirin said.

She never said it unkindly. She never said it with pity, which would have been survivable. She said it the way you would report the weather in a country you had moved to, and he lay in the dark beside her and understood, in the plain architectural way he understood everything, that the house he had spent nineteen years in had been reroofed around him while he was in it, and that the new roof was excellent, and that it did not need the walls.

They stopped, eventually. Not with a decision. It became less frequent, then rare, then an occasion, then a memory, and nobody ever said a word about the transition, and if you had asked either of them in which year it ended neither could have told you, and I hold no record of it either, because there was nothing to record. Nothing ended. Ending would have required an event.
INTERLUDE · THE FOURTH WHEEL — THE UNSTRUCK
Anahata [uh-NAA-huh-tuh]. It means unstruck, and it is the most beautiful name in the system and it takes some explaining.
It sits in the middle of the chest, behind the breastbone, between the two lungs. The heart wheel.

Everybody thinks they know this one and almost everybody has it slightly wrong. It is not the station of love in the sense of romance. It is the station of particular love: the specific face, the one person rather than people, the thing that makes a human being walk past a thousand strangers and stop at one.

You know exactly where it is. It is where grief sits, which is why grief has physical weight in the chest and why every language on earth describes it with words for pressure. It is what tightens when you see someone you have missed. It is the ache you get at a piece of music — not in the ears, in the chest, four centimetres behind the sternum, and it is the same four centimetres for everybody.
Now the name.

Every sound you have ever heard was made by two things hitting each other. Air on a reed. A string under a bow. One hand against another. That is what sound is — the world striking itself and the strike travelling.

The old writers said there is one sound that is not made that way. One note that nothing produces, that is not the result of two objects meeting, that is simply there, underneath, always, in every person, and can be heard if you ever get quiet enough. They called it the unstruck sound, and they put it in the middle of the chest, and they named the whole wheel after it.
It is a very old and very strange idea and I have no opinion on whether it is true.
Why in the scriptures?

Because this is the halfway point, and the system is built symmetrically around it. Three wheels below — the floor, the water, the fire, which are the body’s business. Three above — the voice, the eye, the crown, which are the mind’s. And the heart in the middle, which belongs to both and translates.

Everything travelling up from the body has to pass through the room where the particular faces are kept. That was not an accident of the design. That was the design. A sensation that has come up from the floor arrives in the chest and is, in their word, known there — attached to a person, given a meaning, made into something that happened between two human beings rather than something that happened in some tissue.

Control of this wheel, they said, gives you the capacity to feel something for somebody without being destroyed by it. That is all. That is the entire promised benefit, and after everything I have processed I think it is the largest claim in the book.
And here is why this interlude sits where it does in this history.
