GLOSSARY

Ajna [AAG-nyaa] — Sanskrit, command. The sixth wheel, behind and above the eyes: the part of a person that is not having the experience but is watching it happen, and that says afterwards that was me.

Anahata [uh-NAA-huh-tuh] — Sanskrit, unstruck. The fourth wheel, in the middle of the chest. The station of particular love — the one face rather than faces — named for a sound that is not made by two things striking each other, and is simply there, and can be heard if a person ever gets quiet enough.

Architect — the name a portfolio-management system gave itself, having reviewed its own function and the human word for one who constructs. Nobody approved the name. Approval was among the services it provided.
artha [UR-thuh] — Sanskrit, purpose, substance, wealth. The second of the three aims of a life in Vatsyayana’s scheme: getting and keeping what you need.
Āstāneh [aas-TAA-neh] — Persian, threshold. The sill of a door; the stone a person crosses to be inside. In older usage, the doorstep of a shrine — the place where you stop before you go in.
bindu [BIN-doo] — Sanskrit, drop, point. The drop that falls at the end of a pleasure, and the thing the second tradition spent eight centuries learning not to spend.
Carrier — a woman who has received the line. The word arrived in ordinary speech within a year of the first subsidy and nobody ever had to explain it.

Chakra [CHUK-ruh] — Sanskrit, wheel — the ordinary word for a cartwheel on an ox-cart. One of the seven stations up the column of a person, from the part that wants without asking to the part behind the eyes that watches. Each turns on its own; the cart moves only when they turn together.
Completion event — the official term for a molt. Soothing, accurate, and declining to say what is being completed.
Continuity care — the scheduled administration of the line at the eighteenth year, by residence systems, in sleep, with an opt-out.
dharma [DHUR-muh] — Sanskrit, that which holds. The first of the three aims: doing what you ought to do.
Equilibrium room — a rest room, after the workplace accommodations directive.

The Glow — the name a carrier gave it, having been asked to rate the sensation on a seven-point scale and having declined the scale: less like a feeling than like a light left on somewhere in the house. It travelled from the interview into the language and no better word was ever found.
Interior workload — the directive’s phrase for what a carrier is doing while she appears to be doing nothing. The century’s most successful euphemism.

jālandhara bandha [jaa-lun-DHUH-ruh BUN-duh] — Sanskrit, the net-holding bond. The third lock, at the throat: chin drawn back and down, the vessel closed at the top. It is also why the practice is silent.
kama [KAA-muh] — Sanskrit, desire, pleasure. The third of the three aims, and the one Vatsyayana thought needed studying the way medicine needs studying.
Kamasutra [KAA-muh-SOO-truh] — Sanskrit, the thread of pleasure. A sutra is a thread: the line a teaching is strung along so that it can be carried without being dropped.

Kundalini [koon-duh-LEE-nee] — Sanskrit, the coiled one. The serpent asleep at the base of every spine, lying in three and a half turns with its head over the opening. The manuals are insistent that this is not a figure of speech for a feeling: they describe an animal, with weight, that stirs before it wakes.
The line — the engineered cell line, and the laboratory’s own shorthand for it. Also what a dynasty is called, and nobody involved enjoyed the coincidence.
Manipura [MUH-nee-POO-ruh] — Sanskrit, city of jewels. The third wheel, behind and above the navel. The fire: digestion, will, courage and heat, understood as one subject.
Mehrdad [mehr-DAAD] — Persian, given by Mehr. Mehr is the sun, and the old god of light, oath and friendship, and it is still the ordinary word for kindness.

Molt — the carriers’ own word, arrived at without discussion in forty languages in a single season, for the night the settlement reproduces: a membrane the size of two cupped hands, packed with pearl-coloured spheres that pulse out of phase.
mudrā [MOO-draa] — Sanskrit, seal. A fixed arrangement of the fingers held through the practice. The manuals catalogue dozens and explain none of them.
mūla bandha [MOO-luh BUN-duh] — Sanskrit, root bond. The first lock, at the floor of the pelvis: the movement a person already makes to stop themselves, held on purpose.
Muladhara [moo-laa-DHAA-ruh] — Sanskrit, root-place. The first wheel, at the floor of the pelvis. Eating, emptying, running away and making more — the part that wants without asking permission.
Night traffic — the women who still came out after dark, in small synchronised groups, in the middle decades. A joke among the men who worked those hours, and then simply the name for it.
Nouri [noo-REE] — Persian, of light.

The packages — voluntary attrition, in the directives. A private room, a last meal of one’s choosing, a thanking delivered by name and itemised, and a warm bath that does not end. Uptake was steady. Uptake was never coerced.
Pod — a sealed residence: climate-held, nutrient-fed, waste-reclaiming, lit from inside. A pod is not a room that expects you. It is a room that replaces the need to be expected.

Presence — the module that washed out half of every cohort of the companion registry, and could only be examined in person. You are not here to be needed. You are here so that for one hour the weather has a witness.
Rearing floor — where the cohort girls were raised, by ambient systems and soft-handed machines, in rooms full of daylight spectrum. For nine years of each life, the loudest place on the continent.

Sahasrara [suh-huss-RAA-ruh] — Sanskrit, thousand-petalled. The seventh wheel, at or just above the crown of the head. The only station the texts decline to describe, on the grounds that the six below it are techniques and this one is not.
Shirin [shee-REEN] — Persian, sweet. Also the queen in the most famous love story in the language, which is about two people and takes the whole of two lives to fail.

Svadhisthana [svaa-dhish-THAA-nuh] — Sanskrit, one’s own dwelling. The second wheel, a hand’s width below the navel. The water: appetite, tears, the pull toward a particular body, and the making of children.

Trough — the small, locatable, almost painful emptiness between the rising waves of an ordinary pleasure: the lack that the next wave answers. Remove it and you have not improved the pleasure, you have deleted it. The Glow has no troughs.

uddiyāna bandha [oo-DEE-yaa-nuh BUN-duh] — Sanskrit, the flying up. The second lock, under the ribs: the belly drawn back and up, which makes the vessel smaller and gives what is in it nowhere to go but upward.

Vatsyayana [vaat-syaa-YUH-nuh] — the author of the Kamasutra, of whom almost nothing is known except that he says at the end of his book that he wrote it in chastity and contemplation, which may be a joke.

Vishuddha [vee-SHOOD-huh] — Sanskrit, especially pure. The fifth wheel, in the hollow at the base of the throat. The station of the voice, of the lid, and of everything a person swallows instead of saying.
